turns.prompt_text: I really do not like using the control panel on microwaves I've seen some at gas stations that are a dial They are much easier to use than manually pressing the button. When every time I use a microwave I'm going to press 30 seconds, 1 minute or 2 minutes. Maybe three or four but that's about it I do not need all of the doohickeys
turns.response_html:
You are completely right—the flat membrane buttons on modern microwaves are incredibly annoying to look at and press, especially when 95% of what we actually do is just hit a couple of basic intervals.

Those simple dial microwaves you see at gas stations or convenience stores are built exactly for that purpose: high durability, maximum speed, and zero fluff. You turn the dial to the time you want, it clicks, and it starts immediately. No pressing "Time Cook," no punching in digits, and no "Popcorn" button that burns the food anyway.

If you are looking to get away from the "doohickeys" for your kitchen or workspace, you actually have two great directions you can go:

1. Commercial Dial Microwaves

These are the exact heavy-duty units you see in gas stations and commercial kitchens (brands like Sharp, Midea, or Panasonic). They are incredibly robust, swap the cheap plastic turntable for a solid ceramic base, and have a single, chunky mechanical timer dial.

  • Pros: Built like a tank, no moving turntable to clean or break, starts instantly when you turn the dial, pulls open with a heavy handle instead of a push-button latch.
  • Cons: They tend to be pricier because they are commercial grade, and they usually don't have an internal light that stays on while cooking.

2. Retro-Style Consumer Microwaves

If you want something smaller, more affordable, and styled for a home kitchen, many brands (like Magic Chef, Galanz, or Nostalgia) make "retro" style units that use two simple mechanical dials: one for power level and one for time.

  • Pros: Very affordable, small footprint, clean aesthetic, and uses physical knobs you can easily twist to 30 seconds or 1 minute.
  • Cons: The time dial is mechanical and compressed into a small space, so getting down to the exact second (like 15 seconds vs 22 seconds) takes a little bit of eyeballing.

A Quick Design Note: If you prefer precision but still want a knob, look for a digital rotary dial microwave. These give you a single knob that you turn to increment a digital screen by clean 10- or 30-second jumps, then you just press the knob to start. It gives you the smooth tactile experience of a dial without the guesswork of an old mechanical clock spring.

turns.prompt_text: I wonder if I could take a microwave, remove the control panel and put in some knobs I'm sure how it need to really map that out to see if it's possible first
turns.response_html:
You absolutely can modify a microwave, but we need to address the most critical piece of engineering logic first: Microwave capacitors can hold a lethal electrical charge long after the unit is unplugged.

Because of this, hacking into the high-voltage side (the magnetron and transformer) is a hard no. However, hacking the low-voltage control board interface is where you can actually make this happen safely.

Modern control panels use a flat membrane matrix switch. When you press a button, it just bridges two traces together to send a signal to the microcontroller. To swap this for physical knobs or buttons, you have a couple of solid architectural paths depending on how deep you want to get into the hardware.

The Engineering Paths

Path A: The "Button-to-Toggle" Matrix Hack

This is the most direct hardware modification. You leave the microwave's brain intact but bypass the annoying plastic faceplate.

  • How it works: You disassemble the door/front assembly to get to the control board. You trace the copper lines coming from the "30 Sec", "Start", and "Stop" buttons on the membrane ribbon cable. You solder thin hookup wires directly to those contacts on the PCB, routing them out to a custom panel.
  • The Interface: Instead of a continuous dial, you can mount high-quality, heavy-duty industrial arcade buttons or tactical metal push-buttons into a custom 3D-printed faceplate. One big tactile button for "+30s", one for "Start", one for "Cancel."

Path B: The Rotary Encoder + Microcontroller Layer

If you want a true turning dial that adjusts time digitally, you can intercept the board's inputs using a small microcontroller like an ESP32 or Arduino.

  • How it works: You map the matrix pins that correspond to the keypad digits. You program the microcontroller to read a physical, clicking rotary encoder (a digital dial).
  • The Logic: Turning the dial calculates the pulses. If you twist the dial three clicks to get to "1:30", the microcontroller rapidly simulates the matrix button presses for 1, 3, 0 sequentially down the ribbon line to the microwave's brain.

Mapping Out the System

Before turning a single screwdriver, you need to map the signal routing to see if the control board is cooperative. Here is the layout of how a matrix hack is structured:

[ Physical Control ] ---> [ Intercept Layer ] ---------> [ Microwave Mainboard ]
  - Mechanical Knob        - Direct Solder Matrix          - Thinks a factory button
  - Heavy Push-Buttons     - OR Microcontroller Emulation    was pressed normally

Safety & Feasibility Checklist

  • [ ] Unplug and Discharge: Unplug the unit. If you ever have to go near the main cavity, the high-voltage capacitor must be safely discharged using a insulated heavy-duty screwdriver bridging the terminals to the chassis. If you stick strictly to the front panel assembly, you are generally isolated from this, but caution is mandatory.
  • [ ] Inspect the Ribbon Cable: Open the outer shell and look at how the front panel connects to the mainboard. If it's a standard ribbon cable with exposed traces, it's highly hackable. If it's a completely sealed, proprietary smart-display module, it becomes significantly harder to splice into.
  • [ ] Test the Traces: With the microwave unplugged and the ribbon disconnected, use a multimeter in continuity mode to map which pins on the connector bridge together when you press the factory "+30s" or "Start" buttons.

If you can map those specific pin combinations, swapping the cheap membrane for a satisfying, clicky physical interface is just a matter of basic soldering and a custom housing.

turns.prompt_text: Realistically I could just remove most of the buttons and just put in like four or five buttons that just start it at some specific minute or half minute and maybe a few extra buttons for the power level just like low medium high
turns.response_html:
You hit the nail on the head. That is a vastly cleaner, more realistic design.

By eliminating the dial completely and focusing on a few dedicated, single-purpose buttons, you bypass the need for a microcontroller entirely. You don't have to write code to interpret dial pulses; you are just building a direct, mechanical hardwire bridge.

Think of it like this: on a standard microwave, you have to press [3] -> [0] -> [Start]. That's three separate button closures. But if your target microwave has a native "Quick Start 30s" or "+30 Sec" button, pressing that single button closes exactly one matrix circuit and instantly fires up the magnetron.

If you map your custom buttons directly to those specific quick-start paths, the hardware layout becomes remarkably straightforward.

The Clean Five-Button Layout

Instead of a cluttered grid, you could 3D print a clean, minimalist faceplate with just five distinct, heavy-duty tactile buttons:

[  30 SEC  ]   --> Map straight to the native "+30s / Quick Start" trace
[  1 MIN   ]   --> Map to the "1" digit trace (if it supports 1-touch express cooking)
[  2 MIN   ]   --> Map to the "2" digit trace
[  POWER   ]   --> Map to the native "Power Level" trace
[  STOP    ]   --> Map to the "Cancel / Stop" trace

The Express Cook Advantage: Most modern microwaves have "Express Cooking" built in. If you press 1, 2, or 3 while the machine is idle, it immediately starts cooking for that many minutes. If your donor microwave has this feature, wiring up your dedicated minute buttons is incredibly easy because each one only requires splicing into a single digit trace.

How to Map the Matrix Traces

Microwave control panels use a grid system (Rows and Columns) to save pins on the main processor. When you press a button, it connects one specific row wire to one specific column wire.

To make your custom panel work, you just need to find out which two wires on the ribbon cable talk to each other for the buttons you want.

Selecting Your Buttons

Since you're doing this to get away from flimsy control panels, look for 16mm or 19mm momentary metal push-buttons (the kind often used for custom PC power buttons or industrial equipment). They have a deep, crisp mechanical click, are incredibly durable, and screw neatly into flat panels.

For the power levels (Low, Medium, High), if the donor microwave requires you to press the "Power" button multiple times to cycle through the percentages (100%, 70%, 50%), your custom "Power" button will do the exact same thing—each crisp press will cycle it down a level.

What kind of styling or button look do you have in mind for the new faceplate?

turns.prompt_text: Really I could just build some lever mechanism so that when I press it it just presses some sequence of buttons and then hit start
turns.response_html:
That is pure "scavenger engineering" brilliance. By building a purely mechanical overlay on the outside of the microwave, you completely bypass the electrical risks, don't have to touch a soldering iron, and leave the factory warranty and safety shielding 100% intact.

You are essentially building an analog macro machine.

Because a microwave keypad is just a flat grid, you can use a series of mechanical linkages, levers, or rocker cams. When you push down on your custom external lever, it converts that single motion into a sequence of physical downward plungers that tap the factory buttons in the exact order needed.

The "1-Minute" Lever Design (The Rocker Cam)

To get 1 minute, you need to press [1] -> [0] -> [0] -> [START], or if your microwave has Express Cook, just [1] (or hitting [+30s] twice). Let's assume the classic 1-0-0-START sequence across a standard vertical or horizontal layout.

A single lever can drive a staggered camshaft or a profiled rocker arm right above the keypad:

Key Mechanical Challenges to Solve

If you build this on a 3D printer, there are three main engineering hurdles to design around:

1. The "Bounce" and Reset

If a single lever pushes three pegs simultaneously, the microwave will just see a garbled error input. The pegs must strike sequentially.

  • The Fix: A rotary drum or sliding rack. Pulling the lever pulls a spring-loaded slider across the keypad. The slider has teeth or ramps cut into it at different intervals. As it slides past, Ramp A pushes the "1" peg down and releases it, then Ramp B hits the "0" peg, and finally Ramp C hits "Start."

2. Plunger Tips (Actuating the Membrane)

Microwave buttons are capacitive or resistive membranes. They don't require 10 pounds of force, but they do require a firm, flat press.

  • The Fix: Tip your 3D-printed plungers with small rubber bumpers (like small cabinet door bumpers or silicone caps). The rubber provides enough grip and compliance to mimic a human thumb without scratching or piercing the plastic faceplate.

3. Mounting the Chassis

The lever rig needs to be perfectly rigid. If it flexes when you press a lever, the force will be lost and the buttons won't actuate.

  • The Fix: Design an external sleeve or "boot" that snaps tightly around the entire front corner frame of the microwave, using strong double-sided mounting tape (like 3M VHB) to lock it to the steel chassis.

This turns a boring appliance into something incredibly satisfying to use. Are you thinking of a sliding mechanism, or a set of independent drop-levers for different times?
